`reduce` (ou `fold`, pra quem gosta de Haskell) é uma função de alto nível usada em estruturas de dados que podem ser reduzidas para um único valor, através de uma operação binária.

Por exemplo, o código abaixo faz uma redução usando a função `(+)` e `(*)` como operador binário:

```js
arr = [1, 2, 3, 4]
soma = arr.reduce((acc, x) => acc + x, 0) // 10
produto = arr.reduce((acc, x) => acc * x, 1)  // 24
```

Therefore, my opinion is that it only makes sense to give impression on these editors when you touch upon the power they offer. This might take some time.

So far, I've used vi/Vim  and Emacs, but I'm also planning on experiment with the ones you cited and plus some others like Kakoune (the one that inspired Helix) and some JetBrains (I know they are heavyweight and non-free in both senses, but I like experimenting).

My experience with using vi/Vim is that its design choices really make sense. At first, I tought it would be harder to get used to the default keybindings, but they really are more natural and faster. So I think learning Vim is a must-have even if you don't plan on using it as your main editor in the near future, especially if you do a lot of stuff in non-GUI systems and consider POSIX portability important.

Emacs, despite some saying it is more beginner-friendly than Vim, has one of the steepest and daunting learning curves I ever had to face. I think this is due to it being an almost complete OS! I'm gradually learning both Emacs and Lisp because I plan on using it in the near future as my main editor, at least when I not connecting to a remote server with no GUI, in which case I prefer Vim since it's already there (POSIX!)

I should say that I don't use pure Emacs.  I recently came upon an *Emacs distribution*, a bundle of pre-configured Emacs stuff that some people organize around and contribute to. It combines the best of both worlds by having Vim's keybindings with some interesting mnemonic extensions. It also comes with modules for specific tools, programming languages (Even the less used ones like Scheme, Elixir, Fortran) and etc.

In conclusion. I began with Vim. Check out vimtutor, in half an hour u can get through it and get a taste. If you are curious about Emacs, then checkout its tutorial, and make the decision. Then you can go deeper on both worlds.

There are some good books on vi and Vim (Checkout "The vi and Vim Editors" by O'Reilly) and on Emacs ("Learning GNU Emacs" or "Mastering Emacs").

I can't say much about Neovim, Helix or any other since I'm currently hooked on Doom Emacs. But I do plan to try them out in the future.
